messages.subject: Re: basic logistic regression
parts:
A few thoughts on the logit model from the user's perspective:

1. It will be great when we can run from R. Then the data files will look much cleaner.

2. I assume that it would be ok for us to have "100" rather than "100.0" in the normal distributions?

3. I'm asssuming we can also have declaration statements such as double b_0_scalar, b_dem, b_laborcomm, ... rather than needing a separate line for each?

4. For naive users such as myself, would it be useful to have "real" alias for "double"? I'm assuming all our reals are actually double-precision, i.e. there's no "single" category, so it could be convenient to have "real" with the manual noting that it's an alias for "double". Or am I missing something there?

5. At very first look the declarations make the model look awkward, but now that I look carefully they're pretty clear.

6. Would it make sense to allow the declarations and the model to be split into 2 different files? In most cases it probably makes sense to have them all in one place, but I'm thinking of two settings where it might be convenient to have the declarations in one place and the model in another:

(a) Suppose we have a model that we're running in different ways: sometimes we're doing inference for theta given y, other times we're forward-simulating y from theta, other times we're simulating everything from the prior, etc. In that case, different runs have different breakdowns of data/parameters, but the model is not changing and it could be convenient to keep the model fixed and swap in different declaration blocks.

(b) Suppose we're fitting many different models from the same data. Then it would be convenient to have a single data declaration and parameters block, and to swap in different models. In this sort of setting, it would be important to (i) allow us to declare data that are not actually used in the model, and (ii) allow us to declare parameters that are not in the model. I assume that (i) is trivial with Stan; (ii) might be slighlty harder but I still think should be do-able?

See you
A

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: basic logistic regression
parts:
On Feb 11, 9:16 pm, Bob Carpenter <c...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> On 2/11/12 9:10 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> > 4.  For naive users such as myself, would it be useful to have "real" alias for "double"?  I'm assuming all our reals are actually double-precision, i.e. there's no "single" category, so it could be convenient to have "real" with the manual noting that it's an alias for "double".  Or am I missing something there?
>
> I'd rather just call it one thing rather than have
> two aliases.  I'm happy to go with real.  There isn't
> going to be single-precision or quadruple-precision options.

I agree that having multiple names for the same thing is not good. My
fav help page in all of R is help(double) .

Also, if stan is 100% templated, why not support at least as many
precisions as Eigen does? Not that anyone should want single
precision, but someone might want *more* precision. In other words,
one way out of the problem we are facing with this logit model might
be to do

model {
long double mu;
for (i in 1:I) {
mu = b_0 + b_1 * x_1[i] + b_2 * x_2[i] ... ;
y[i] ~ bernoulli(inv_logit(mu));
}
}

That is not a very good solution because long double is highly
compiler dependent; see

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_double

And if I change inv_logit() to use expl() instead of exp(), it doesn't
help noticeably under g++. But it was a plausible idea.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: basic logistic regression
parts:
Adding precision to a Stan model is an interesting
idea. It would be easier to support at the whole
model level than variable by variable (a problem
with the latter being Eigen's not wanting to do
things like multiply double matrices by float
or long double matrices). I haven't templated out
the double type, but it'd be relatively straightforward.

I like the idea of calling it "real" rather than
"double" in the code.

The problem is exp(x), which for doubles, only allows a
domain of x in roughly (-750,750). Values of x that
are too small result in underflow to 0 and
too big result in overflow to +infinity.
This means that

inv_logit(x) = 1/(1+exp(-x))

inherits the same domain for x, but where under-
and over-flow result in 0 or 1 values.

For logistic regression, the problem is that we
don't get that much additional range going from
64 to 128 bits. It only increases the exponent
from 11 bits to 15 bits, which gives us log(2**4)
or about triple the range, or around (-2000,2000).
We do get a whole lot more precision in the base
number, though :-)

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: "real" it is
parts:
"double" isn't any more jargony than "real".
Both have specific meanings and "double" is
more accurate in this case. Real
numbers are a mathematical concept whereas
double-precision floating point is an approximate
implementation. The Stan variables declared
as doubles are implemented as doubles.

Having said that, I like the idea of expressing
the models mathematically and letting the Stan
compiler sort out the implementation details.
As Ben pointed out, we could always change the
nature of our real-number approximation without
changing the Stan code.

So, "real" it is.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: "real" it is
parts:
If the type is now intended to refer to a mathematical field rather
than the way the thing is stored on a computer, then we should
probably say integer in .stan files rather than int. Of course, the
vector, matrix, cov_matrix, etc. types don't explicitly refer to a
field but in statistical software I doubt anyone would think they they
held anything other than real numbers in them.

Ben
